Notes: Op./Kryl./Iter.: precision (bits) of the operator, the Krylov vectors and the iterate; 32/64 = FP32 storage with FP64 element arithmetic. Steps: Krylov steps (IR: outer/inner). FP64 true residual: ||b-Ku||/||b|| of the returned iterate from an independent FP64 checker. Factor per step: (r_end/r_0)^(1/n) of FP64 true residuals, n = Krylov steps (IR: inner steps). Solve: our paths, median of three timed solves (original-stencil IR: none timed, as its solves broke down). The number of timed solves of each released code followed its own prespecified rule: for Hou et al.'s code it was fixed by grid size (three timed solves at 8.19M elements, median 164.8 s; one at 33.6M); for the released OpenMP-offload code it was set by duration (three solves when the first took at most 120 s, otherwise that one solve; at 8.19M, three at S1 and one at S5). Step: synchronized time per Krylov step (ours: interval between successive preconditioner calls, IR within an outer step; Hou: between iteration starts; released OpenMP code: between iteration ends). Memory: dedicated GPU memory of the job (a: from a separate run with one build and one solve, outside the prespecified protocol; the prespecified memory comparison, from the timed processes, which retain two builds, is inconclusive, so this column gives no confirmatory memory ordering; Hou's value is mostly reserved pool memory and depends on the pool cap of that run; by live allocation (pool used) Hou's 4.74 GB lies between FP64 PCG's 6.46 GB and IR's 4.43 GB; the released OpenMP code: growth of the WSL virtual-machine process). b: per-step times of the released code come from its timing build, which ran 10% faster than the plain build. c: iteration cap of the released code. Neither released code reaches 1e-5 at any checked iterate, so every time ratio in this table is at unequal accuracy.

Notes: Sizes are active elements. Verified: an independent FP64 residual <= 1e-5 at the returned iterate. a: the two assembled-matrix studies used different admission rules for the build: the operator survey required three times the estimated matrix storage to fit the free memory, the update-cost study 1.15 times (its fused build allocates only the matrix arrays); both refusals are predictions, not measured limits. b: at 33.6M and 65.5M elements the independent check is missing for every path, because the checker did not fit, so the accuracy relationship there is unresolved; the released code's allocated grid at 65.5M active elements has 79.6M elements. State S1 is the released first design state, solved from zero; state S5 is the density of the released fifth solve, solved from the released fourth solution. The 65.5M completions hold for S1 only. c: historical completions (the submitted paper's records), not results of the prespecified protocol. At the same size the prespecified runs fared as stated: for repaired IR and the recursive-stop control at 113.2M, not admitted because the predicted workspace plus 1.5 GiB exceeded the guard's effective free-memory estimate (the smaller of the driver-reported free memory and the total memory less the other processes' dedicated use); a prediction, not a measured limit. For FP64 PCG at 65.5M, an allocation failure in design iteration 3 under the pool cap of that protocol. For the recursive-stop control, a run outside the admission rule (not a lower bound) completed the cantilever at 113.2M. The paper-wide maximum is unchanged. d: on the fixed states, the predicted peak plus 1.5 GiB exceeded the free memory the driver reported; a prediction, not a measured limit. e: a state S5 exists only where the released design loop completed its first four design iterations. At 33.6M that loop was interrupted at its run-time cap, which also counted its in-loop transfers of whole vectors to the host; it was not run above that size, so no S5 state exists at 33.6M or above, and the matched-rule loops had no released loop to start from.

Interference: no whole-solve time is excludable under the 5% rule; that bound covers whole solves only. u: at the duration of one Krylov step the 5% rule is unresolved (released, 0.52M, S1: about 14.3%); the other step times meet it at step duration. The activity bounds cover the GPU processes present when the activity sampler started; the records neither establish coverage of a process created later nor show that one interfered.

Coefficients: in the operator survey every operator of a row applies the same modulus field, so each comparison uses identical coefficients. In the update-cost study the stencil was timed on a modulus field E and the sparse product on a second field E2 drawn from the same distribution (the matrix is built from E, refreshed to E2, then timed). The two studies used the same assembled-matrix classes; they differ in the admission rule for the build, so each refusal is a prediction under its own rule, not a measured limit.
